fact: Many birds build nests to hold eggs and protect chicks.
Eagles build large nests of sticks called eyries.
Hummingbirds build tiny cup nests using plant fibers and spider silk.
Weaver birds knot grass into hanging woven nests.
Many penguins raise chicks in large groups called colonies.
Rabbits dig underground burrows for shelter and raising young.
Prairie dogs live in connected underground burrow systems called towns.
Foxes use dens for resting and raising kits.
Wolf pups are often born in sheltered dens.
Bears use dens for winter shelter and to raise newborn cubs.
Badgers live in underground homes called setts.
Meerkats dig complex burrows with many entrances.
Moles dig underground tunnels while searching for food.
Groundhogs build burrows with separate chambers.
Ants build colonies with tunnels and chambers underground or in wood.
Some termites build tall mounds that help control temperature inside.
Honey bees live together in hives filled with wax comb.
Paper wasps build nests from chewed wood fibers.
Many spiders spin silk webs to catch food or protect eggs.
Silkworm caterpillars spin silk cocoons before becoming moths.
Many butterflies transform inside a chrysalis.
A snail carries a hard shell that protects its soft body.
Hermit crabs move into empty shells for protection.
A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton.
Armadillos dig burrows to rest and escape heat.
Beavers build lodges from sticks mud and vegetation.
Muskrats build dome-shaped lodges in wetlands.
An otter's resting den can be called a holt.
Platypuses dig riverbank burrows for resting and nesting.
Crocodiles lay eggs in nests made of sand or vegetation.
Alligators build mound nests from plants and mud.
Sea turtles bury their eggs in sandy beach nests.
Many frogs lay eggs in ponds or other freshwater habitats.
Many salamanders shelter under damp logs and rocks.
Coral reefs provide hiding places and food for many fish.
Clownfish shelter among the tentacles of sea anemones.
Octopuses hide in rocky dens and may decorate the entrance with shells.
Moray eels often rest in narrow cracks in coral reefs.
Lobsters shelter in rocky crevices during the day.
Seahorses use their tails to grip seagrass and coral.
Pregnant polar bears dig snow dens where cubs are born.
Arctic fox families may reuse the same den for many years.
Many penguins nest on stones or sheltered ice-free ground rather than building nests from ice.
Some seals keep breathing holes open in sea ice.
Walruses rest together on beaches or floating ice called haul-outs.
Many bats roost in caves trees or buildings.
Some owls nest in natural hollows inside trees.
A squirrel's leafy tree nest is called a drey.
Woodpeckers carve nest cavities into tree trunks.
Raccoons often sleep in hollow trees or sheltered dens.
Koalas spend much of their lives resting and feeding in eucalyptus trees.
Orangutans build new sleeping nests from branches and leaves.
Gorillas make simple sleeping nests from leaves and branches.
Chimpanzees often build sleeping nests high in trees.
Lions rest in shaded grassland areas within their pride's territory.
Elephants travel to water holes to drink bathe and cool off.
Giraffes live in open savannas and woodlands where tall trees grow.
Camels rest in desert shade and are adapted to hot dry habitats.
Mountain goats live on steep rocky slopes that help protect them from predators.
Puffins often nest in burrows or rocky crevices near the sea.
